prompt: Many patients do not follow the advice they are given by their doctors. Why does this happen? What are the consequences of this behaviour?
essay:
Studies of prescribed treatment consistently find that a large proportion of patients stop taking medication early or never begin it at all. The behaviour looks irrational from the outside, but it usually has understandable causes, and its consequences reach well beyond the individual concerned.

The commonest cause is that the reasoning behind the advice is never transmitted. A consultation lasting a few minutes leaves time to issue an instruction but not to explain why a course of antibiotics must be finished, or why blood-pressure tablets are needed by somebody who feels perfectly well. Advice that arrives without a reason is easy to abandon as soon as the symptoms disappear.

Two further causes matter. Side effects are experienced immediately while the benefit of treatment is invisible and delayed, so a patient weighing certain nausea against a hypothetical stroke in twenty years often decides against the medicine. And where the advice requires a change of habits rather than a tablet — losing weight, giving up alcohol, exercising daily — compliance demands sustained effort in an environment that offers very little support for it.

The consequences are serious at both levels. For the patient, a partially treated condition frequently returns in a worse form, and admission to hospital costs far more, in suffering as well as money, than the treatment that was declined. For the health system, non-adherence wastes the medicines dispensed, fills beds that need not have been filled, and drives the spread of drug-resistant infection when antibiotic courses are abandoned halfway. There is also a slower effect on the consultation itself, since doctors who expect their advice to be ignored tend to invest less in explaining it.

Non-adherence is therefore best understood not as stubbornness but as a predictable response to advice that has been issued rather than explained.
title: Why patients ignore their doctors
